newsitem.title: USA: Danka buys Kodak office copier business.
newsitem.headline: Danka buys Kodak office copier business.

text.p: Britain's Danka Business Systems Plc will acquire the sales, marketing and equipment service operations of Eastman Kodak Co.'s office copier business for $684 million in cash, the companies said Monday.

The companies will also form a strategic alliance under which Kodak will supply high volume copiers and printers to Danka, making the British-based company the principal distributor of Kodak-branded office copiers and printers.

Kodak will retain manufacturing and research and development functions supporting its office imaging business. Kodak will also retain its key colour electrophotography technology for use in its other imaging businesses.
Around 10,400 Kodak employees will be offered employment by Danka, with some 6,000 located in the United States.

Monday's deal is just the latest bit of corporate trimming at Kodak, which has spun off and sold businesses, generating some $8 billion. The company has in the 1990s exited pharmaceuticals, household goods and chemicals.
News of the deal boosted Danka's American Depositary Receipts, which jumped $6.625, or 22 percent, to close at $36.50 on Nasdaq. Kodak closed at $71.75, down 50 cents, on the New York Stock Exchange.
The deal will make Danka a one-stop shop for office copiers and printers worldwide, while expanding the market for Rochester, N.Y.-based Kodak's products.

"This strategic alliance will allow Danka to offer customers a unique combination of unparalleled service and support with global coverage, as well as a wide choice in equipment -- from small copiers to high-volume duplicators, fax machines and state-of-the art digital copiers/printers," said Dan Doyle, chief executive officer of Danka.
"This alliance promises to increase access to the market for Kodak-branded office imaging products," said Kodak's assistant chief operating officer, Carl Kohrt.

"In addition, Danka's acquisition of our sales, marketing, and facilities management operations will place our sales and service people in a growing organisation that is devoted exclusively to providing solutions for the office."

The deal makes Danka a leading provider of photocopiers than can handle a high humber of pages per minute -- the fastest-growing segment of the business, which accounts for 43 percent of the North American market. Kodak is one of only three manufacturers of high-volume photocopiers and the only one to allow distribution by third parties.
The sale prompted copier leader Xerox Corp. to throw down the gauntlet.

"They're on our turf now and are going to have to chase us to win business," said Gill Hatch, a Xerox vice vresident, who predicted the Danka-Kodak deal will bring pricing pressures to the copier business.
"Suffice to say that Danka has been aggressive, and will continue to be aggressive," he said.
Danka is already one of the largest and fastest-growing independent suppliers of automated office equipment and related service and supplies in North America, Europe, Australia and New Zealand.
The deal should bring Danka's yearly sales to about $3.5 billion and double its recurring revenues from copier service, supplies and rentals to more than $2 billion.
The company, whose U.S. operations are based in St. Petersburg, Fla., will have 22,000 employees in more than 700 offices in 35 countries.
Kodak said the transaction would result in a charge of about $250 million in the quarter in which it closes and in net cash proceeds of $600 million.
"This transaction will be accretive to the company's on-going earnings," Harry Kavetas, Kodak's chief financial officer, said in an interview.
He said the manufacturing operation Kodak will retain is expected to achieve operational profits by the end of 1997.
The parties plan to close the deal by the end of 1996, subject to approval by Danka shareholders and regulators.
